result.markdown: --- title: "Probabilistic numerical integration" subtitle: "Appendix A06 · error bars on the ODE solve" course-unit: a05-probabilistic-numerical-integration status: complete --- ## Why this unit matters - Every numerical ODE solve is an approximation, yet a classical solver returns a single trajectory with **no statement of its own error**. - *Probabilistic numerics* reframes integration as Bayesian inference: the solver returns a **distribution** over trajectories whose spread reflects the discretisation uncertainty [@bosch2021]. - Here we make that uncertainty **concrete and executable** by measuring the true error of a coarse solve against a near-exact reference. ::: {.notes} The deck delivers the concept with a fully runnable deterministic core, and documents — but does not execute — the current probabilistic-solver API, because of a real package-compatibility gap flagged on the next slide. ::: ## Reproducibility gate: `ProbNumDiffEq.jl` > The pinned `ProbNumDiffEq.jl` v0.17 does **not** precompile against the > resolved `OrdinaryDiffEq` stack — `OrdinaryDiffEqDifferentiation` no longer > exposes the `standardtag` symbol its solvers reference: > > ``` > UndefVarError: `standardtag` not defined in `OrdinaryDiffEqDifferentiation` > ``` - We therefore **gate** the probabilistic solve (`eval: false`) and run an **executable error-quantification core** with the standard stack. - The gated block reflects the *current* v0.17 API, verified against the installed source, so it runs as written once the packages are realigned. ::: {.notes} Show the load error, then move on quickly: the point of the session is the quantity, not the packaging. The deterministic core teaches exactly what the filter's posterior standard deviation is designed to estimate, which is time-varying numerical error. ::: ## Model and the quantity of interest Baseline SIR (unchanged): $S(0)=990,\,I(0)=10,\,R(0)=0,\,N=1000$, $c=10$, $\beta=0.05$, $\gamma=0.25$ — **deterministic**, continuous in time and state. $$ \frac{dS}{dt} = -\beta c\frac{SI}{N},\quad \frac{dI}{dt} = \beta c\frac{SI}{N} - \gamma I,\quad \frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I . $$ - Numerical error $e(t) = \hat u(t) - u(t)$ cannot be evaluated exactly, but we approximate $u(t)$ to machine precision with a tight, high-order solve. - A probabilistic solver models $e(t)$ **online** as a Gauss–Markov process; its posterior standard deviation $\sigma(t)$ is a calibrated proxy for $|e(t)|$. ::: {.notes} Keep the classification line consistent with the rest of the course. The key idea is that probabilistic numerics does not change the model — it changes the solver's *output type* from a point to a Gaussian. ::: ## Measuring the error directly ::: {#cell-fig-a06-slide-error .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using EpiModelingCourse, OrdinaryDiffEq, CairoMakie p = BASELINE_PARAMETERS; s0 = BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE u0 = [s0.S, s0.I, s0.R]; tspan = (0.0, 40.0); δt = 0.5 prob = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p) ref = solve(prob, Vern9(); abstol = 1e-12, reltol = 1e-12, saveat = δt) coarse = solve(prob, Tsit5(); abstol = 1e-1, reltol = 1e-1, saveat = δt) err = abs.(reduce(hcat, coarse.u) .- reduce(hcat, ref.u)) fig = Figure(size = (820, 400)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "absolute error", yscale = log10, title = "Numerical error vs. reference") for (i, (lab, col)) in enumerate(zip(("S", "I", "R"), (:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen))) lines!(ax, ref.t, max.(err[i, :], 1e-10); color = col, linewidth = 2, label = lab) end axislegend(ax; position = :rb) fig ``` ::: {#fig-a06-slide-error .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Absolute error of a coarse-tolerance Tsit5 solve against a machine-precision Vern9 reference. Error peaks through the epidemic maximum, where the vector field changes fastest — exactly what a probabilistic solver would report as a wider posterior. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} The error is not uniform in time — it is largest around the peak. A filtering solver would widen its posterior there and narrow it in the slow tails, guiding adaptive effort. This time-structure is the whole point. ::: ## Calibration check & the gated API ::: {#a06-slide-refine .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Printf refm = reduce(hcat, ref.u) for tol in (1e-1, 1e-3, 1e-5, 1e-7) s = solve(prob, Tsit5(); abstol = tol, reltol = tol, saveat = δt) e = maximum(abs.(reduce(hcat, s.u)[2, :] .- refm[2, :])) @printf("tol = %.0e → max |I error| = %.3e\n", tol, e) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` tol = 1e-01 → max |I error| = 8.627e-01 tol = 1e-03 → max |I error| = 7.748e-03 tol = 1e-05 → max |I error| = 3.187e-04 tol = 1e-07 → max |I error| = 3.619e-06 ``` ::: ::: Tightening tolerance monotonically shrinks the error — the deterministic analogue of a probabilistic solver reporting smaller uncertainty at smaller steps. The **gated** current API (not run here): ```julia using ProbNumDiffEq, Statistics sol = solve(prob, EK1(order = 3, prior = IWP(3), diffusionmodel = DynamicDiffusion(), smooth = true); dt = 0.5, abstol = 1e-1, reltol = 1e-2) std(sol(20.0)) # calibrated error, no reference needed ProbNumDiffEq.sample(sol, 100) # draws from the solver's posterior ``` ::: {.notes} The refinement table is the calibration story in deterministic form: a useful probabilistic solver must have its reported standard deviation track this true error. Exercise 2 asks students to reason about IWP order, EK0 vs EK1, and the diffusion model against this backdrop. ::: ## Key takeaways & caveats - **Uncertainty is largest where dynamics are fastest** — around the epidemic peak. - **Calibration is the whole point** — the reported $\sigma$ must bracket the true error; the refinement check is that question, deterministically. - **Cost** — filters carry a covariance alongside the state; the payoff is an error bar, rarely worth it for routine forward simulation. - **Where it matters** — when solver error could be mistaken for model error, e.g. likelihood-based inference with coarse solves. - **Environment caveat** — the probabilistic solve is gated by a package-compatibility gap, *not* by the method. See the [book chapter](../../appendices/05-probabilistic-numerical-integration.html) and the [ProbNumDiffEq.jl](https://nathanaelbosch.github.io/ProbNumDiffEq.jl/stable/) and [SciML ODE](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/) documentation. ::: {.notes} End by pointing to the companion notebook, which lets the audience slide the coarse tolerance and the output step and watch the measured error respond — the interactive version of the calibration argument. :::
